speaker: Boris Cherny
title: Head of Claude Code: What happens after coding is solved | Boris Cherny
question: In agentic coding workflows, why does switching to a cheaper, smaller model often fail to reduce total task cost?
guest: One tip I find pretty useful is to just use the most capable model—currently Opus 4.6, with maximum effort enabled always. The thing that happens is sometimes people try to use a less expensive model like Sonnet, but because it's less intelligent, it actually takes more tokens in the end to do the same task. So it's actually not obvious that it's cheaper if you use a less expensive model. Often it's actually cheaper and less token-intensive if you use the most capable model, because it can do the same thing much faster with less correction and less hand-holding.

points.core: Less intelligent models burn more total tokens completing the same task.
points.note: Accept: Weaker models take extra turns, dead ends, retries, or verbose back-and-forth, inflating total token consumption on complex coding tasks. Do not credit: Generic claims that cheaper models have lower quality without connecting to higher total token consumption.

points.core: Capable frontier models finish tasks faster with far less human hand-holding.
points.note: Accept: Stronger models solve problems in fewer iterations with minimal steering or correction overhead from the engineer. Do not credit: Generic praise of frontier models being 'smarter' or 'more accurate' without linking to reduced correction/steering overhead.

points.core: Lower per-token rates frequently yield higher overall spend on complex tasks.
points.note: Accept: Unit token price is misleading because total task cost equals price per token times total tokens consumed, making the premium model cheaper end-to-end. Do not credit: Both-sides hedging that 'it depends on the task' without clearly stating the per-token vs. total-cost inversion.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Because total cost is price per token multiplied by tokens consumed, and smaller models tend to consume far more tokens to finish the same task. A lower per-token price only helps if the token count stays roughly constant, and in agentic loops it usually doesn't.

Weaker models make more mistakes per step: wrong edits, misread errors, bad tool calls, and poor plans. Each mistake triggers extra turns of retrying, re-reading files, and re-running tests. Since every turn resends the accumulated conversation context as input, costs compound: a task that takes twice as many turns can cost much more than twice the tokens. Errors also cascade, because an early wrong assumption poisons later steps and can force large rework.

On top of that, smaller models fail outright more often. A failed run costs its tokens and still leaves the task undone, so you pay again for a rerun, escalation to a larger model, or human debugging and review time, which usually dwarfs the API bill.

The meaningful metric is therefore cost per successfully completed task, not cost per token. Small models do save money on simple, well-scoped subtasks where they reliably succeed.

models.label: Gemini 4 Carbon
models.answer:
In agentic coding workflows, total cost depends on cumulative token volume across an entire trajectory rather than per-token pricing alone. Because an agent resends its growing conversation history—file reads, tool schemas, and command outputs—on every turn, input token consumption compounds roughly quadratically with step count. Smaller, cheaper models plan and reason less accurately, causing them to inspect irrelevant files, misdiagnose root causes, and write flawed patches that trigger long test-and-fix retry loops. Each extra turn repeatedly bills an increasingly bloated context window, quickly erasing the lower unit price even when prompt caching discounts repeated prefixes.

That exploratory noise also pollutes the context window, further degrading the smaller model's accuracy and increasing output generation as the session drags on. Measured as expected cost per *solved* task, weaker models fare worse still: they fail outright far more often, burning tokens on dead-end runs that ultimately require restarts, developer cleanup, or fallback to a frontier model that could have finished cleanly in a few turns.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer: Agentic tasks are billed per token over the whole trajectory, not per call, so the price per token is only one factor. A smaller model usually needs more turns to finish the same task. It makes more mistakes, misreads tool output, retries failed edits, reruns tests and wanders through dead ends. Each extra turn resends the growing context of files, logs and earlier messages, so the input tokens add up roughly quadratically with the number of steps. A model that costs a fifth as much per token but takes three to five times as many steps, with bigger contexts, can cost the same or more in total. It can also fail outright, and then you pay for the wasted run plus a retry, often on the bigger model anyway. There are hidden costs too: weaker models write longer, less focused reasoning, cache prompts less efficiently because of churn, and leave subtle bugs that cost human review time later. Stronger models tend to solve problems in fewer, more decisive steps. What matters is the cost per successfully completed task, not the cost per token.

models.label: Gemini 4 Neon
models.answer: In agentic coding workflows, total cost is driven not just by per-token pricing, but by how many turns and tokens it takes to reach a working solution. Cheaper, smaller models frequently cost as much or more overall because they make more errors—misinterpreting requirements, misusing tools, hallucinating APIs, or introducing bugs that fail tests. Each mistake forces additional edit-and-debug iterations, and because every turn in an agentic loop typically re-sends the accumulated conversation history, file contents, and error logs, token consumption grows rapidly with each extra step. Smaller models also tend to navigate codebases less efficiently, reading irrelevant files or running redundant commands that bloat the context window and degrade reasoning further. In the worst case, they get stuck in loops and fail to complete the task, wasting the entire run before a stronger model or developer has to take over. A pricier frontier model that plans accurately and resolves the task in a few clean turns often ends up cheaper in practice.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
A cheaper model lowers the price per token, but the cost of an agentic coding task depends on how much work it takes to finish. A smaller model may need more turns to understand the codebase, make more tool calls, or spend more time fixing mistakes and rerunning tests. Each extra turn can also add input cost as the conversation and tool outputs grow.

The savings can disappear entirely if the smaller model gets stuck and a stronger model has to redo the work. The useful metric is cost per successfully completed task, including retries and escalations. Smaller models can still save money on well-scoped tasks they reliably finish in roughly the same number of steps.
